pos: adv./adj. (sixty times over; a measure of abundant yield)
etymology: From sixty + -fold, Old English -feald, denoting multiplication or repetition; sixtyfold names a yield multiplied sixty times beyond what was sown.
biblical_def:
But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.

Christ's parable of the sower describes four kinds of soil receiving the identical seed, the word of the kingdom, with three of the four producing no lasting fruit at all — the wayside, the stony ground, and the thorns each defeat the seed in a different way. Only the good ground bears fruit, and even among the good ground the yield varies: hundredfold, sixtyfold, thirtyfold. Christ's own explanation (Matthew 13:18-23) identifies the good ground as the one who heareth the word, and understandeth it, bringing forth fruit as the inevitable mark of genuine reception, while the varying yield shows that fruitfulness itself admits real degrees without any believer being written off as unfruitful soil. Sixtyfold sits between the greatest and least recorded yield, a reminder that Scripture measures fruit by abundance relative to the seed sown, not by uniform output across every believer. The parable's center of gravity is not the exact ratio but the contrast between fruit and no fruit at all; where the word takes root in an understanding, believing heart, fruit of some multiplied measure is the certain and promised result.

webster_full: FOLD, (combining form) Denoting multiplication or repetition by the number prefixed.
SIXTYFOLD, a./adv. Sixty times as much; multiplied sixty times over.

The temptation it answers is a live one in the church: measuring one's own fruitfulness against another believer's hundredfold yield and concluding that a sixtyfold or thirtyfold harvest is failure. The parable names all three as genuine, multiplied fruit from good ground; the line that actually divides is not between sixtyfold and hundredfold but between fruit and no fruit at all.

pos: adj. (consisting of three strands or parts; multiplied three times)
etymology: From three + -fold, Old English -feald; a threefold cord is one twisted of three strands rather than one or two.
biblical_def:
And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

Ecclesiastes closes a meditation on the goodness of companionship with this proverb of cordage: a single strand is easily snapped, two strands resist better, but a cord twisted of three strands withstands what would break the others. The surrounding verses commend two working together, lifting one another up, and warming one another against the cold — the plain, practical goods of human companionship against the futility the Preacher has traced throughout the book. The threefold cord caps the argument by moving past mere pairing to a stronger multiplication of the same principle, and interpreters have long seen room, without forcing the text past its plain sense, to read a third strand as the LORD Himself bound together with two companions, since Ecclesiastes elsewhere insists that labor, companionship, and enjoyment are all gifts receivable only from God's hand. Whether the third strand is read narrowly as a third companion or more broadly as God present in the bond, the proverb's force is the same: strength multiplies with proper, godly-ordered companionship far beyond what isolation can ever produce.

pos: adv. (in the second place; next in order of appointment)
etymology: From second, Latin secundus, following, + the adverbial -ly; secondarily marks a position in a deliberately ordered sequence.
biblical_def:
And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.

Paul closes his great treatment of spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 with this ordered list, and the ordinal markers — first, secondarily, thirdly — are deliberate rather than decorative. God hath set some in the church: the gifts and offices named are not achievements believers seize for themselves but appointments the Sovereign Lord Himself assigns, each member placed by divine design the way He has placed eyes, ears, and hands in a physical body in the verses just before. Secondarily names prophets as the second-ranked office in this particular list, following apostles and preceding teachers, within a church still receiving direct apostolic and prophetic foundation; the ranking concerns function and order within the body, not personal worth before God, since the chapter's entire argument has just been that the humbler members of the body are no less necessary or honored than the prominent ones. The ordered list answers the Corinthian church's disordered scramble for the most visible gifts, especially tongues, by reasserting that the Lord who gives every gift also orders their use.

webster_full: SECOND, a. Next after the first in order, place, time, or rank.
SECONDARILY, adv. In the second place; following the first in a deliberate sequence.

pos: adv. (in the third place; next after the second in order)
etymology: From third, Old English thridda, + the adverbial -ly; thirdly marks the third position in an enumerated, ordered list.
biblical_def:
And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.

Thirdly completes the opening triad of Paul's ordered list in 1 Corinthians 12:28, placing teachers immediately after apostles and prophets and ahead of miracles, healings, helps, governments, and tongues. The sequence is instructive on its own terms: the word-centered offices — apostles who laid the church's foundation, prophets who spoke immediate revelation in the apostolic age, and teachers who steadily instruct the church in that revealed word — are named first, before any of the more visibly dramatic gifts that follow. Teachers remain a standing office in the church long after the apostolic and prophetic foundation has closed, continuing the pattern Ephesians 4:11 calls pastors and teachers, charged with building up the saints through sound instruction in the word already given. Thirdly's position in the list is therefore not a demotion but a statement of priority: ongoing, faithful teaching of Scripture ranks with the foundational offices as essential and honored, standing ahead of the more spectacular gifts the Corinthian church was prone to overvalue.

pos: adv. (without settled aim or assurance; in a manner lacking fixed direction)
etymology: From un-, not, + certain, from Latin certus, fixed or sure, + the adverbial -ly; to run uncertainly is to run without a fixed goal in view.
biblical_def:
I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air.

Paul has just compared the Christian life to the discipline of athletes at the games, who undergo rigorous, temperate training for a prize that perishes, while believers run for an incorruptible crown. Not as uncertainly denies that his own race lacks a fixed object; he keeps the finish line, the prize of faithful ministry and final glory, constantly in view, and disciplines his body accordingly rather than running without aim or direction. The parallel image, beateth the air, pictures a boxer throwing wild, purposeless blows that never connect with an actual opponent, all effort and no effect. Paul applies both images to himself specifically in the verses following, where he speaks of keeping under his body and bringing it into subjection lest, after preaching to others, he himself should become a castaway. Uncertainly therefore names the opposite of the disciplined, purposeful, self-denying Christian life Paul commends: not legalistic uncertainty about salvation, which Paul elsewhere denies absolutely, but the wasted, undirected effort of a life, even a ministry, that never actually presses toward its appointed goal.

webster_full: UNCERTAIN, a. Not certain; doubtful; not sure or fixed.

etymology: From un-, not, + perfect, from Latin perfectus, completed or finished; unperfect names a state not yet brought to completion, distinct from the moral sense sinful imperfection often carries.
biblical_def:
Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.

David's meditation on the LORD's intimate knowledge of him reaches back before birth, even before formation was complete, to a stage the Authorized Version calls unperfect — not sinful or deficient in the moral sense, but simply unfinished, still being fashioned in the womb. The verse insists that God's eyes saw this unformed substance and that his book, the register of providence, already contained all my members before any of them existed in finished form. This is among Scripture's clearest statements that personal identity, known and recorded by God, begins before birth and before physical completion, grounding the doctrine that the unborn are already the objects of the LORD's intimate knowledge and providential care, not merely potential persons awaiting some later threshold. David's confession that such knowledge is too wonderful for me; I cannot attain unto it closes the psalm's opening movement in worship rather than mere biological observation, treating God's knowledge of the unperfect, unformed body as a ground for praise and for the sanctity of life at every stage, from unformed substance onward.

pos: adj. (swift to come; executed without delay)
etymology: From Old English sped, success or haste, + -y; speedy names that which arrives or is accomplished without delay.
biblical_def:
Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD'S wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a speedy riddance of all them that dwell in the land.

Zephaniah's opening oracle announces the great day of the LORD's wrath against Judah's idolatry and complacency, and this verse closes the chapter with a warning that wealth, the usual refuge of the secure and self-satisfied, will prove powerless on that day. Speedy riddance intensifies the threat: judgment will not merely come eventually but swiftly, decisively, leaving no interval for last-minute escape by purchased security. The surrounding oracle names those who say in their heart, the LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil, a practical atheism that assumes divine inaction regardless of covenant unfaithfulness; the speedy riddance answers that assumption directly. Zephaniah's day of the LORD language becomes a template the prophets and the New Testament both reuse for final judgment, and the speed named here is not haste without warning, since the prophet has just finished warning at length, but the swift certainty with which judgment executes once the appointed day finally arrives, after a period of patient warning the complacent chose not to heed.

etymology: From Latin taedium, weariness or disgust, through Old French tedieux; that which is tedious wearies the hearer through its length rather than its content.
biblical_def:
Notwithstanding, that I be not further tedious unto thee, I pray thee that thou wouldest hear us of thy clemency a few words.

The orator Tertullus opens the Jewish leaders' accusation against Paul before the Roman governor Felix with calculated flattery, praising Felix's provision of quietness and worthy deeds, then promising brevity so as not to be tedious to a busy official, before launching into the charge that Paul is a mover of sedition and a ringleader of a sect. The courtroom flattery is itself worth noting as a pattern Scripture records without endorsing: smooth, self-interested rhetoric designed to win a hearing before the actual substance, often thin, is delivered. Paul's own response (verses 10 and following) dispenses with such flattery and answers the charges plainly and factually, appealing to his own conduct and to the resurrection hope he shares with his accusers' own law and prophets. Tedious here names nothing about Paul or the gospel; it names Tertullus's own rhetorical strategy, a reminder that smooth speech promising not to be tedious can precede an accusation with very little substance behind it, and that plain, factual testimony, as Paul gives, remains the Christian's proper answer to such accusation.

pos: adv. (in a manner marked by lavish, costly expense)
etymology: From Latin sumptus, expense or cost, from sumere, to take or spend; to fare sumptuously is to live at great, self-indulgent cost.
biblical_def:
There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day.

Christ's parable opens with a deliberately stark contrast: a rich man clothed in purple and fine linen, fared sumptuously every day, set immediately beside Lazarus, a beggar full of sores laid at the rich man's gate desiring the crumbs that fell from his table. The rich man's sumptuous daily feasting is not condemned by the parable for wealth as such, since Abraham himself was wealthy and is named as the one who receives Lazarus into comfort; the condemnation falls on a self-indulgent abundance that walked past suffering at its own gate every single day without mercy. The reversal that follows death — Lazarus comforted in Abraham's bosom, the rich man in torment, a great gulf fixed between them — makes plain that sumptuous living purchased at the cost of ignored mercy carries eternal consequence, not merely social imbalance. The rich man's later plea for Lazarus to warn his brothers is refused on the ground that they have Moses and the prophets already, a warning Christ's hearers, with Moses and the prophets likewise in hand, were meant to feel directed at themselves.

pos: adj. (dignified and imposing in manner or appearance; marked by grandeur)
etymology: From state, Latin status, standing or condition, + -ly; stately names a grandeur befitting high rank or office, whether rightly or wrongly assumed.
biblical_def:
And satest upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it, whereupon thou hast set mine incense and mine oil.

Ezekiel 23 indicts Jerusalem, figured as an adulterous woman named Aholibah, for pursuing idolatrous alliances and worship with the same imagery the prophets use elsewhere for spiritual harlotry. The stately bed in this verse is no innocent furnishing; it is the setting for an idolatrous feast at which incense and oil that properly belonged to the LORD alone, consecrated for His worship, were instead spread before false gods and foreign lovers. The grandeur the word stately names is precisely the problem: Jerusalem dressed her unfaithfulness in the trappings of dignity and luxury, making apostasy look splendid rather than shameful. Scripture repeatedly exposes this pattern, that idolatry rarely presents itself as degraded or ugly; it is staged with stately beds, prepared tables, and stolen incense, borrowing the very glory that belongs to the LORD to dress up rebellion against Him. The indictment that follows in the chapter is severe precisely because the sin was committed with such evident, self-assured splendor rather than furtive shame.

webster_full: STATE, n. Condition; rank; dignity; also, pomp or grandeur of appearance.

Illustrates the recurring pattern of idolatry staged with borrowed, stolen glory.
scriptures: And satest upon a stately bed, and a table prepared before it, whereupon thou hast set mine incense and mine oil.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that idolatry and spiritual unfaithfulness routinely present themselves with dignity and splendor rather than visible shame, and must be judged by their substance, not their staging.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word remains in ordinary, unaltered use.

The pattern Ezekiel exposes is still live wherever compromise, false worship, or unfaithfulness to God is dressed in cultural dignity, aesthetic polish, or social prestige. Stately staging never changes the substance of what is offered on the bed; incense and oil belonging to the LORD, given to another, remain stolen worship however splendid the table prepared for it.
roots_summary: From Latin status, standing or condition, state and stately name dignity or grandeur; Ezekiel 23:41 uses it of the splendid staging of Jerusalem's idolatrous unfaithfulness.
roots_lines: Status, Latin for standing or condition, underlies state and stately.
Names dignified, imposing grandeur, whether rightly or wrongly assumed.
Ezekiel 23:41 pictures Jerusalem's idolatry staged upon a stately bed.
Incense and oil belonging to the LORD are instead given to false gods.
Illustrates idolatry's recurring pattern of splendid, dignified staging.
